original_question: Fix c>0. Among isotropic composites made from an elastic phase and void, which microstructures in two and/or three dimensions maximize the quantity mu* - c kappa*, or at least form a sequence of microstructures whose values of mu* - c kappa* converge to the supremum?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Problem 4.3: the open problem of finding, for fixed c>0, isotropic elastic-phase/void microstructures in 2D and/or 3D that maximize μ*−cκ*, or else a maximizing sequence if the optimum is not attained. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core of the paper's official formulation: c is fixed and positive; the constituents are an elastic phase and void; the admissible objects are isotropic microstructures/composites; the dimensional scope is two and/or three dimensions; and the goal is either an optimizer for μ*−cκ* or a sequence whose values approach the best possible value. That is essentially Problem 4.3 in §4. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
missing_details: The draft does not explicitly define κ* and μ* as the effective bulk and effective shear moduli of the resulting isotropic composite. The nearby context introduces exactly this notation. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

It does not explicitly state that the nonvoid constituent is a fixed isotropic elastic material with positive bulk modulus κ and shear modulus μ, while the second phase is void. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

It does not say that the search is over isotropic microstructures themselves, not merely over arbitrary composites whose effective tensor happens to be isotropic. Problem 4.3 is phrased in terms of isotropic microstructures. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

It does not make explicit that the paper poses the problem in dimension d=2 and/or d=3, i.e. separately as an open problem in either or both of those dimensions, rather than as a single uniform theorem across all d. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

It does not mention the immediate motivating context from Problem 4.2: the elementary bounds 0≤κ*≤κ and 0≤μ*≤μ imply μ*−cκ*≤μ, and the paper asks whether this can be improved or whether one can approach (κ*,μ*)=(0,μ). ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

It does not say that no phase volume fraction is specified in the statement as written; a stand-alone version should therefore avoid adding a fixed-volume-fraction constraint that the paper does not include here. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

It does not note the large-c interpretation given immediately afterward: this becomes the search for the 'ultimate auxetic material', namely maximal μ* under κ* arbitrarily close to 0. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

Algebraic items such as ambient ring/field, homogeneity degree, and nilpotency conditions are not part of this problem's formulation; the stand-alone rewrite should not invent such restrictions. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
refined_question: Fix c>0 and a nonvoid isotropic elastic phase with bulk modulus κ>0 and shear modulus μ>0. In dimension d=2 and/or d=3, among all isotropic microstructures made from this elastic phase and void, identify those whose effective bulk and shear moduli (κ*,μ*) make μ*−cκ* as large as possible; if no maximizing microstructure exists, construct a sequence of isotropic microstructures whose effective moduli satisfy μ*−cκ*→ the largest possible value. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
justification: The draft is targeting §4, not the paper's earlier conjectural material: the surrounding discussion defines κ* and μ* for isotropic composites of a fixed isotropic elastic phase and void, records the elementary bounds (4.1), then states Problem 4.2 about improving μ*−cκ*≤μ, and immediately follows with Problem 4.3 asking for the isotropic microstructures that maximize that same linear functional. The next paragraph explains that very large c corresponds to maximizing μ* subject to κ* being arbitrarily close to zero, which is why the problem is presented as part of the search for an 'ultimate auxetic material.' Problem 4.4 is only a narrower large-c specialization in 2D, so your draft is best matched by Problem 4.3 itself. The paper does not explicitly present any theorem proving an equivalent reformulation of Problem 4.3, so the correct alternate-formulation field is null. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
